sources.title: Trust Region Policy Optimization
sources.authors: John Schulman, Sergey Levine, Philipp Moritz, Michael I. Jordan, Pieter Abbeel
sources.authority: The originating paper of the trust-region policy-gradient line (TRPO), which PPO and GRPO descend from; names the algorithm Aman wrote as "TRPO".

facts.claim: TRPO is an iterative policy-optimization procedure with a monotonic-improvement guarantee in theory; the practical algorithm approximates the theory.
facts.quote: We describe an iterative procedure for optimizing policies, with guaranteed monotonic improvement.

facts.claim: Theory uses a penalty on total-variation distance (Theorem 1, via Eq. 9); the recommended penalty coefficient from theory gives very small steps, which motivates a constraint instead.
facts.quote: In practice, if we used the penalty coefficient C recommended by the theory above, the step sizes would be very small.

facts.claim: The trust-region form: constrain KL between old and new policy rather than penalize it.
facts.quote: One way to take larger steps in a robust way is to use a constraint on the KL divergence between the new policy and the old policy, i.e., a trust region constraint

facts.claim: The max-KL constraint over all states is impractical; the practical algorithm uses the average KL (Eq. 12).
facts.quote: Instead, we can use a heuristic approximation which considers the average KL divergence

facts.claim: Optimization is second-order-flavoured: conjugate gradient plus a line search, costing only slightly more than the gradient itself.
facts.quote: We use the conjugate gradient algorithm followed by a line search, which is altogether only slightly more expensive than computing the gradient itself.

facts.claim: Two sampling schemes: single-path (model-free) and vine (needs resettable states).
facts.quote: We describe two variants of this algorithm: first, the single-path method, which can be applied in the model-free setting; second, the vine method

facts.claim: Step size used in all experiments: KL bound delta = 0.01.
facts.quote: We used δ = 0.01 for all experiments.

facts.claim: TRPO is described as similar to natural policy gradient methods.
facts.quote: This algorithm is similar to natural policy gradient methods and is effective for optimizing large nonlinear policies such as neural networks.

sources.title: High-Dimensional Continuous Control Using Generalized Advantage Estimation
sources.authors: John Schulman, Philipp Moritz, Sergey Levine, Michael I. Jordan, Pieter Abbeel
sources.authority: Defines GAE(gamma, lambda), the advantage estimator inside PPO-for-LLMs; the quantity GRPO-family methods replace with group-relative baselines.

facts.claim: GAE reduces policy-gradient variance using a value function, at the cost of some bias, via an exponentially-weighted estimator analogous to TD(lambda).
facts.quote: We address the first challenge by using value functions to substantially reduce the variance of policy gradient estimates at the cost of some bias, with an exponentially-weighted estimator of the advantage function that is analogous to TD(λ).

facts.claim: Both gamma and lambda trade off bias and variance; lambda is the knob specific to GAE.
facts.quote: both of which contribute to the bias-variance tradeoff when using an approximate value function

facts.claim: Best values found in the paper lie in narrow ranges.

sources.title: Proximal Policy Optimization Algorithms
sources.authors: John Schulman, Filip Wolski, Prafulla Dhariwal, Alec Radford, Oleg Klimov
sources.authority: The PPO paper; the RL algorithm in InstructGPT and the base that GRPO modifies.

facts.claim: PPO alternates sampling with optimizing a surrogate objective over multiple minibatch epochs; positioned as TRPO-like benefits with much simpler implementation.
facts.quote: The new methods, which we call proximal policy optimization (PPO), have some of the benefits of trust region policy optimization (TRPO), but they are much simpler to implement, more general, and have better sample complexity (empirically).

facts.claim: The clipped objective L^CLIP = E[min(r_t A_t, clip(r_t, 1-eps, 1+eps) A_t)] with eps = 0.2 as the suggested value.
facts.quote: where epsilon is a hyperparameter, say,

facts.claim: The min makes the clipped objective a pessimistic (lower) bound on the unclipped objective; the ratio change is ignored only when it would improve the objective.
facts.quote: so the final objective is a lower bound (i.e., a pessimistic bound) on the unclipped objective.

facts.claim: The adaptive-KL-penalty variant performed worse than clipping; included as a baseline.
facts.quote: In our experiments, we found that the KL penalty performed worse than the clipped surrogate objective

facts.claim: Reference hyperparameters (MuJoCo, 1M timesteps): horizon 2048, Adam stepsize 3e-4, 10 epochs, minibatch 64, gamma 0.99, GAE lambda 0.95.
facts.quote: Horizon (T) Adam stepsize Num. epochs Minibatch size Discount (γ) GAE parameter (λ)

sources.title: Approximating KL Divergence
sources.authors: John Schulman
sources.authority: The primary source for the k1/k2/k3 KL estimators; the "K3 estimator (Schulman, 2020)" that GRPO, DeepSeek-V3.2 and TRL use for the KL-to-reference term. Author is a PPO/TRPO author.

facts.claim: k1 = -log r is unbiased but high variance because it is negative for half the samples.
facts.quote: However, it has high-variance, as it’s negative for half of the samples, whereas KL is always positive.

facts.claim: k2 = (1/2)(log r)^2 is low variance but biased; its expectation is an f-divergence that matches KL to second order.
facts.quote: An alternative estimator, which has lower variance but is biased, is

facts.claim: k3 = (r - 1) - log r is unbiased and always non-negative (distance between log and its tangent).
facts.quote: This leaves us with the estimator k_3 = (r - 1) - \log

facts.claim: Numerical check, q=N(0,1), p=N(0.1,1), true KL 0.005: k1 bias/true 0, stdev/true 20; k2 0.002, 1.42; k3 0, 1.42. For true KL 0.5 (p=N(1,1)): k1 0, 2; k2 0.25, 1.73; k3 0, 1.7.
facts.quote: k3 has even lower standard deviation than k2 while being unbiased, so it appears to be a strictly better estimator.

facts.claim: Reverse-direction estimator for KL[p,q]: r log r - (r - 1).
facts.quote: r \log r - (r - 1)

conflicts: S45 (DeepSeek-V3.2 §3.1) shows the K3 estimator, while unbiased for the value, has a biased gradient when sampled tokens are far less probable under pi_theta than pi_ref, and corrects it with an importance ratio. The blog analyses estimator value, not gradient.

facts.claim: Headline result: a 1.3B InstructGPT model is preferred to 175B GPT-3 by labelers, with >100x fewer parameters.
facts.quote: outputs from the 1.3B parameter InstructGPT model are preferred to outputs from the 175B GPT-3, despite having over 100x fewer parameters.

facts.claim: Labeler team: about 40 contractors screened for sensitivity to different preferences.
facts.quote: We first hire a team of 40 contractors to label

facts.quote: The SFT dataset contains about 13k training prompts (from the API and labeler-written), the RM dataset has 33k training prompts (from the API and labeler-written), and the PPO dataset has 31k training prompts (only from the API).

facts.quote: we found that 175B RM training could be unstable and thus was less suitable to be used as the value function during RL

facts.claim: RL is a bandit environment: random prompt in, response out, reward from RM ends the episode; per-token KL penalty from the SFT model mitigates overoptimization; value function initialized from the RM.
facts.quote: In addition, we add a per-token KL penalty from the SFT model at each token to mitigate overoptimization of the reward model. The value function is initialized from the RM.

facts.claim: PPO-ptx objective (Eq. 2): RM reward minus beta * log(pi_RL/pi_SFT) plus gamma * pretraining log-likelihood; gamma = 0 gives plain PPO.
facts.quote: The KL reward coefficient, β, and the pretraining loss coefficient, γ, control the strength of the KL penalty and pretraining gradients respectively. For "PPO" models, γ is set to 0.

facts.claim: "Alignment tax": RLHF regresses on SQuAD, DROP, HellaSwag, WMT15 fr-en; mixing pretraining gradients (PPO-ptx) largely removes it without hurting preference scores.
facts.quote: We can greatly reduce the performance regressions on these datasets by mixing PPO updates with updates that increase the log likelihood of the pretraining distribution (PPO-ptx), without compromising labeler preference scores.

sources.title: Direct Preference Optimization: Your Language Model is Secretly a Reward Model
sources.authors: Rafael Rafailov, Archit Sharma, Eric Mitchell, Stefano Ermon, Christopher D. Manning, Chelsea Finn
sources.authority: Originating DPO paper.

facts.claim: DPO reparameterizes the RLHF reward so the optimal policy is closed-form, replacing reward-model fitting plus RL with a classification loss; no sampling from the LM during fine-tuning.
facts.quote: eliminating the need for sampling from the LM during fine-tuning or performing significant hyperparameter tuning.

facts.claim: DPO loss (Eq. 7): -E log sigmoid(beta log pi_theta(y_w|x)/pi_ref(y_w|x) - beta log pi_theta(y_l|x)/pi_ref(y_l|x)). Reward is implicit: r_hat = beta log(pi_theta/pi_ref).
facts.quote: This way, we fit an implicit reward using an alternative parameterization, whose optimal policy is

facts.claim: Gradient reweights each pair by how wrong the implicit reward ordering is.
facts.quote: higher weight when reward estimate is wrong

facts.claim: TL;DR summarization: DPO ~61% win rate at temperature 0.0 vs PPO 57% at its best temperature.
facts.quote: We find that DPO has a win rate of approximately 61% at a temperature of 0.0, exceeding the performance of PPO at 57% at its optimal sampling temperature of 0.0.

facts.claim: Default hyperparameters: beta = 0.1, batch 64, RMSprop, LR 1e-6 with 150-step warmup.
facts.quote: Unless noted otherwise, we use a β = 0.1, batch size of 64 and the RMSprop optimizer with a learning rate of 1e-6 by default.

conflicts: S11 (Xu et al.) argues PPO beats DPO on harder benchmarks; S50 (Llama 3) and S16 (Tulu 3) report DPO competitive at lower cost.

sources.title: KTO: Model Alignment as Prospect Theoretic Optimization
sources.authors: Kawin Ethayarajh, Winnie Xu, Niklas Muennighoff, Dan Jurafsky, Douwe Kiela
sources.version: arXiv v5 (updated 2026-09-08 per arXiv API); ICML 2024
sources.authority: Originating paper for KTO; learns from a binary desirable/undesirable signal rather than pairs.

facts.claim: KTO maximizes the utility of generations (Kahneman-Tversky model) rather than log-likelihood of preferences, and learns from a binary signal.
facts.quote: it matches or exceeds the performance of preference-based methods at scales from 1B to 30B, despite only learning from a binary signal of whether an output is desirable.

facts.claim: Claims no single human-aware loss is universally superior; best loss depends on inductive biases of the setting.
facts.quote: our work suggests that there is no one HALO that is universally superior; the best loss depends on the inductive biases most appropriate for a given setting

sources.title: Mitigating LLM Hallucination via Behaviorally Calibrated Reinforcement Learning
sources.authors: Jiayun Wu, Jiashuo Liu, Zhiyuan Zeng, Tianyang Zhan, et al.
sources.authority: Independent, public work on training LLMs against strictly proper scoring rules with RL - the closest peer-reviewed-style analogue to what TypeSafe asserts RLCD does (S35); complements RLCR (S32).

facts.claim: Argues binary-reward RLVR makes models test-takers that guess whenever correctness probability is above zero.
facts.quote: Standard RLVR paradigms, utilizing binary reward signals, inadvertently incentivize models as good test-takers rather than honest communicators, encouraging guessing whenever correctness probability exceeds zero.

facts.claim: Proposes interventions that optimize strictly proper scoring rules so the model outputs a calibrated probability of correctness, enabling abstention or claim-level flagging.
facts.quote: we propose and evaluate training interventions optimizing strictly proper scoring rules for models to output a calibrated probability of correctness.

facts.claim: Reports a 4B model (Qwen3-4B-Instruct) exceeding GPT-5 on a log-scale Accuracy-to-Hallucination Ratio gain: 0.806 vs 0.207 on BeyondAIME (authors' own evaluation, not independently verified).
facts.quote: our model's log-scale Accuracy-to-Hallucination Ratio gain (0.806) exceeds GPT-5's (0.207) in a challenging in-domain evaluation (BeyondAIME).

sources.title: Is DPO Superior to PPO for LLM Alignment? A Comprehensive Study
sources.authors: Shusheng Xu, Wei Fu, Jiaxuan Gao, Wenjie Ye, et al.
sources.authority: The most-cited head-to-head "DPO vs PPO" study; the pro-PPO side of the offline-vs-online debate.

facts.claim: States the split: deployed products use reward-model + PPO, while academic leaderboards were dominated by DPO.
facts.quote: Novel applications such as ChatGPT and Claude leverage reward-based methods that first learn a reward model and apply actor-critic algorithms, such as Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO). However, in academic benchmarks, state-of-the-art results are often achieved via reward-free methods, such as Direct Preference Optimization (DPO).

facts.claim: Claims DPO has theoretical limitations and that PPO wins on every testbed including code competitions.
facts.quote: Experiment results demonstrate that PPO is able to surpass other alignment methods in all cases and achieve state-of-the-art results in challenging code competitions.

conflicts: S50 (Llama 3 §4.1.4) says the opposite on their stack: PPO needed more compute and did worse than DPO, especially on IFEval. S16 (Tulu 3) found PPO roughly equal to DPO at ~7x the wall-clock.

sources.title: Unpacking DPO and PPO: Disentangling Best Practices for Learning from Preference Feedback
sources.authors: Hamish Ivison, Yizhong Wang, Jiacheng Liu, Zeqiu Wu, et al.
sources.authority: Controlled ablation of data, algorithm, reward model and prompts; the study Tulu 3 cites when choosing DPO for iteration and PPO for RLVR.

facts.claim: Ranking of factors: preference data quality matters most, then algorithm, then reward model, then extra unlabeled prompts.
facts.quote: better preference data leading to the largest improvements, followed by the choice of learning algorithm, the use of improved reward models, and finally the use of additional unlabeled prompts for policy training.

facts.claim: PPO beats DPO by small margins.
facts.quote: Notably, PPO outperforms DPO by up to 2.5% in math and 1.2% in general domains.

conflicts: Gain sizes (2.5% math, 1.2% general) are small relative to the data-quality effect (up to 8%) reported in the same abstract.

sources.title: Back to Basics: Revisiting REINFORCE Style Optimization for Learning from Human Feedback in LLMs
sources.authors: Arash Ahmadian, Chris Cremer, Matthias Gallé, Marzieh Fadaee, Julia Kreutzer, Olivier Pietquin, Ahmet Üstün, Sara Hooker
sources.authority: The critic-free precursor to GRPO: argues PPO is unnecessary for RLHF and proposes REINFORCE Leave-One-Out (RLOO).

facts.claim: Core argument: the reward arrives only for the full generation, so model the whole completion as one action rather than per-token MDP steps.
facts.quote: rewards are only attributed to full generations, with no true rewards for any intermediary tokens in the generation. Thus, it is more appropriate and efficient to model the entire generation as a single action with the initial state determined by the prompt.

facts.claim: Headline claim: vanilla REINFORCE beats PPO; PPO is over-engineered for pre-trained LLMs.
facts.quote: PPO is unnecessarily complicated for a pre-trained LLM environment.

facts.claim: Reported margin: REINFORCE outperforms PPO by 3.2% to 20.3% win-rate across datasets and base models (Llama, Pythia; HH and TL;DR).
facts.quote: is consistently outperforming PPO by 3.2% to 20.3%

facts.claim: RLOO baseline: for each of k samples, the other k-1 samples give an unbiased estimate of expected return for the prompt, "akin to a parameter-free value-function, but estimated at each training step". Cost: more sampling.
facts.quote: akin to a parameter-free value-function, but estimated at each training step

facts.claim: RLOO is claimed to beat PPO, DPO and RAFT on all datasets and models, and to make better use of online samples than RAFT.
facts.quote: we empirically show it consistently outperforms baselines such as PPO, DPO (Rafailov et al., 2023) as well as RAFT (Dong et al., 2023) across all datasets and models.

conflicts: S11 (Xu et al.) concludes the opposite ranking (PPO > DPO and other alternatives); S12 finds PPO > DPO by small margins. RLOO paper does not compare against a tuned value-model PPO of the S11 kind.

sources.title: DeepSeekMath: Pushing the Limits of Mathematical Reasoning in Open Language Models
sources.authors: Zhihong Shao, Peiyi Wang, Qihao Zhu, Runxin Xu, et al.
sources.authority: The paper that introduced GRPO (Feb 2024) - not DeepSeek-R1, which adopted it. Also gives the unified SFT/RFT/DPO/PPO/GRPO gradient view.

facts.claim: GRPO is a PPO variant that drops the critic and takes the baseline from the group of sampled outputs for the same question.
facts.quote: GRPO foregoes the critic model, instead estimating the baseline from group scores

facts.claim: Motivation against PPO: the value model is another policy-sized model (memory + compute), and LLM rewards are given at the last token so a per-token value function is hard to train.
facts.quote: As the value function employed in PPO is typically another model of comparable size as the policy model, it brings a substantial memory and computational burden.

facts.claim: Group-relative advantages match how reward models are trained (comparisons between outputs on the same question).
facts.quote: The group relative way that GRPO leverages to calculate the advantages, aligns well with the comparative nature of rewards models

facts.claim: KL-to-reference is added to the loss, not to the reward as in PPO/InstructGPT, so it does not enter the advantage.
facts.quote: instead of adding KL penalty in the reward, GRPO regularizes by directly adding the KL divergence between the trained policy and the reference policy to the loss, avoiding complicating the calculation of

facts.claim: DeepSeekMath-RL training setup: lr 1e-6, KL coefficient 0.04, 64 outputs per question, max length 1024, batch size 1024, single policy update per exploration stage; about 144K CoT-format questions from GSM8K/MATH SFT data.
facts.quote: The KL coefficient is 0.04. For each question, we sample 64 outputs. The max length is set to 1024, and the training batch size is 1024.

facts.claim: Results from RL on DeepSeekMath-Instruct 7B: GSM8K 82.9% -> 88.2%, MATH 46.8% -> 51.7%, with out-of-domain gains.
Iterative GRPO retrains the reward model on new policy samples with a 10% replay of historical data and resets the reference model to the policy.
facts.quote: continually train the old reward model using a replay mechanism that incorporates 10% of historical data.

facts.claim: Online RFT vs GRPO: GRPO scales its gradient coefficient by reward magnitude, penalizing wrong answers; Online RFT only reinforces correct ones. GRPO beat Online RFT (Fig. 5).
facts.quote: In contrast, Online RFT lacks this feature; it does not penalize incorrect responses and uniformly reinforces all responses with correct answers at the same level of intensity.

facts.claim: RL improved Maj@K but not Pass@K on GSM8K and MATH: authors read this as sharpening the output distribution rather than adding capability. (The seed of the S24 / S23 debate.)
facts.quote: it seems that the improvement is attributed to boosting the correct response from TopK rather than the enhancement of fundamental capabilities.

facts.claim: Unified paradigm: SFT, RFT, DPO, PPO and GRPO are all special cases of one gradient form distinguished by data source, reward function, and gradient coefficient.
facts.quote: we provide a unified paradigm to analyze different training methods, such as SFT, RFT, DPO, PPO, GRPO

conflicts: S18 (Dr. GRPO) shows the 1/|o_i| per-sequence normalization and std division in GRPO introduce length and difficulty biases; S45 (DeepSeek-V3.2) later drops std division.

facts.quote: The reward signal is solely based on the correctness of final predictions against ground-truth answers, without imposing constraints on the reasoning process itself. Notably, we bypass the conventional supervised fine-tuning (SFT) phase before RL training.

facts.claim: GRPO is credited to Shao et al. 2024 and described as simplifying PPO and cutting its resource use.

facts.quote: we introduce a language consistency reward during RL training, which is calculated as the proportion of target language words in the CoT.

facts.claim: Stage-1 RL of R1 prints "GRPO clip ratio epsilon to 10" and says a low clip value truncates gradients while a high one destabilizes. The value 10 differs from the 0.2 convention (S3) - treat as possibly a typo or a different parameterization.
facts.quote: the GRPO clip ratio 𝜀 to 10

facts.claim: SFT data for the final stage: about 600k reasoning samples (rejection sampling from stage-1 RL checkpoint, correct only; some judged by a generative reward model via DeepSeek-V3) + about 200k non-reasoning samples.
facts.quote: In total, we collect about 600k reasoning-related training samples.

The text says R1 took "about 4 days, or roughly 80 hours" - 4 days would be 96 h, so treat 80 h (consistent with the 41K GPU-hours in Table 7) as the figure of record.

facts.claim: Reward hacking observed with the helpful (neural) reward model; reward rose while reasoning performance fell (Figure 6).
facts.quote: we observe such reward hacking behavior when employing the helpful reward model.

facts.claim: Distillation beats small-model RL: on Qwen2.5-32B, 10K+ steps of RL (Qwen2.5-32B-Zero) only matches QwQ-32B-Preview, while distilling R1 is significantly better.

facts.claim: Failed attempts - PRM: step granularity is hard to define, step correctness is hard to judge, and any model-based PRM invites reward hacking.

sources.title: Tulu 3: Pushing Frontiers in Open Language Model Post-Training
sources.authors: Nathan Lambert, Jacob Morrison, Valentina Pyatkin, Shengyi Huang, et al.
sources.authority: Coined and open-sourced RLVR (Nov 2024, two months before R1); fully open recipe with PPO-vs-DPO cost measurements.

facts.claim: RLVR definition: the RLHF objective with the reward model replaced by a verification function; reward is a constant if the completion is verified.
facts.quote: RLVR leverages the existing RLHF objective but replaces the reward model with a verification function

facts.claim: RLVR targets skills with ground-truth outcomes: GSM8K, MATH, and precise instruction following (IFEval-style constraints).
facts.quote: Our results show that RLVR can improve GSM8K, MATH, and IFEval performance.

facts.claim: PPO vs DPO cost in a controlled setup: roughly equal average scores, PPO about 28 h on two nodes vs DPO about 4 h on one node.
facts.quote: The PPO runtime is roughly 28 hours using two nodes, whereas the DPO runtime is about 4 hours using a single node.

facts.claim: Decision recorded: do preference iteration with DPO, reserve PPO for RLVR.
facts.quote: We decide to use PPO primarily for RLVR

facts.claim: Preference-tuning variant chosen: only length-normalized DPO beat the base checkpoint overall among DPO, SimPO and length-normalized DPO.
facts.quote: We found that only length-normalized DPO outperformed our base checkpoint overall

facts.claim: Value model for RLVR PPO is initialized from a general reward model; this gave the best GSM8K and average scores.
facts.quote: Initializing RLVR’s Value Function from a General RM Works Best.

facts.claim: More KL budget does not necessarily improve verifiable reward on GSM8K/MATH; large KL leads to average-score drops (overoptimization).
facts.quote: as the model diverges more from the initial model, overoptimization happens as the average scores drop significantly.

facts.claim: Final RLVR hyperparameters: KL penalty coefficient beta = 0.05 for 8B and 0.07 for 70B (omega is the LR warm-up ratio: 0.0 for 8B, 0.07 for 70B).
facts.quote: The final 8B RLVR model used β = 0.05 and ω = 0.0; the final 70B RLVR model used β = 0.07 and ω = 0.07

facts.claim: RL infrastructure: asynchronous PPO with dedicated vLLM (PagedAttention) inference GPUs via Ray; scaled to 405B.
facts.quote: This setup allowed us to scale PPO policy training to the 405B scale.

facts.claim: 405B RLVR: only the MATH train set; over 5 MATH points gained within 25 steps; trained only 75 steps due to infrastructure scaling difficulty.
facts.quote: even with as few as 25 RLVR steps, MATH performance improved by over 5 points

facts.claim: Named limitation/future work: the 8B value model; value-free methods such as GRPO untested.
facts.quote: Future works can benefit from exploring larger value models or alternate value model-free RL algorithms such as GRPO

conflicts: S11 (Xu et al.) says PPO is stronger than DPO; here PPO was only comparable and 7x slower in wall-clock on the authors' stack.

sources.title: DAPO: An Open-Source LLM Reinforcement Learning System at Scale
sources.authors: Qiying Yu, Zheng Zhang, Ruofei Zhu, Yufeng Yuan, et al.
sources.authority: Source of Clip-Higher, Dynamic Sampling, token-level loss and overlong shaping - the changes TRL (default loss_type=dapo), Olmo 3 and others adopted.

facts.claim: Headline: 50 AIME 2024 points on Qwen2.5-32B base, beating DeepSeek-R1-Zero-Qwen-32B (47) in 50% of the training steps.
facts.quote: outperforming the previous SoTA DeepSeekR1-Zero-Qwen-32B using 50% training steps.

facts.claim: Naive GRPO on the same base reaches only 30 AIME points; problems named: entropy collapse, reward noise, training instability.
facts.quote: the naive GRPO baseline suffers from several key issues such as entropy collapse, reward noise, and training instability

facts.claim: Four techniques: Clip-Higher, Dynamic Sampling, Token-Level Policy Gradient Loss, Overlong Reward Shaping.
facts.quote: 1. Clip-Higher, which promotes the diversity of the system and avoids entropy collapse;

facts.claim: Ablation ladder on AIME24 avg@32: naive GRPO 30; +overlong filtering 36; +clip-higher 38; +soft overlong punishment 41; +token-level loss 42; +dynamic sampling (full DAPO) 50.
facts.quote: Main results of progressive techniques applied to DAPO

facts.claim: Clip-Higher: raise eps_high (0.28) and keep eps_low (0.2); raising the lower bound would crush low-probability tokens to 0 and collapse the sampling space.
facts.quote: We keep εlow as it is, because increasing it will suppress the probability of these tokens to 0, resulting in the collapse of the sampling space.

facts.claim: Dynamic Sampling: oversample and drop prompts whose accuracy is exactly 0 or 1, since all-equal rewards give zero advantage and shrink the effective batch.
facts.quote: A zero advantage results in zero policy gradients, shrinking the magnitude and increasing the noise sensitivity of the batch gradient

facts.claim: Token-level loss: sample-level averaging underweights tokens in long responses and cannot penalize gibberish in long samples.
facts.quote: tokens within longer responses (which contain more tokens) may have a disproportionately lower contribution to the overall loss

facts.claim: KL term removed: for long-CoT reasoning the policy is expected to diverge substantially, so the restriction is unnecessary.
facts.quote: during training the long-CoT reasoning model, the model distribution can diverge significantly from the initial model, thus this restriction is not necessary.

facts.claim: Training details: verl framework; AdamW constant lr 1e-6 with 20-step warmup; prompt batch 512 x 16 responses; minibatch 512 (16 gradient updates per rollout step); 16,384-token expected max + 4,096 soft-penalty cache = 20,480 max generation; AIME evaluated as avg@32 at temperature 1.0, top-p 0.7.
facts.quote: For rollout, the prompt batch size is 512 and we sample 16 responses for each prompt.

conflicts: S23 (ProRL) argues the KL penalty (with periodic reference resets) is a stronger entropy-control tool than DAPO-style tricks when starting from an SFT/distilled checkpoint; DAPO removes KL for base-model RL.
S18 (Dr. GRPO) fixes length bias by a constant normalizer, not token-level averaging.

sources.title: Understanding R1-Zero-Like Training: A Critical Perspective
sources.authors: Zichen Liu, Changyu Chen, Wenjun Li, Penghui Qi, Tianyu Pang, Chao Du, Wee Sun Lee, Min Lin
sources.authority: Source of Dr. GRPO and the length/difficulty-bias analysis of GRPO; also the check on what R1-Zero-style training actually does to base models.

facts.claim: Finds the "aha moment" already in DeepSeek-V3-Base and strong Qwen2.5 behaviour without prompt templates - suggesting pretraining priors drive R1-Zero-like gains.
facts.quote: our analysis reveals that DeepSeek-V3-Base already exhibit “Aha moment”, while Qwen2.5 base models demonstrate strong reasoning capabilities even without prompt templates, suggesting potential pretraining biases.

facts.claim: GRPO has a response-level length bias from dividing by |o_i|: for correct answers shorter ones get larger updates; for wrong answers longer ones are penalized less - so wrong responses grow.
facts.quote: Response-level length bias: This arises from dividing by |oi |.

facts.claim: GRPO has a question-level difficulty bias from dividing by the group reward std: questions that are too easy or too hard get higher weight.
facts.quote: Questions with lower standard deviations (e.g., those that are too easy or too hard, with the outcome rewards being almost all 1 or 0) are given higher weights during policy updates.

facts.claim: The length normalization also appears in open-source PPO implementations (loss normalized by response length), predating GRPO.
facts.quote: all of these implementations normalize the loss by response length

facts.claim: Dr. GRPO removes both the 1/|o_i| and the std normalizations (constant normalizer); result: 43.3% AIME 2024 with a 7B base (Qwen2.5-Math-7B) using a minimalist recipe.
facts.quote: a minimalist R1-Zero recipe that achieves 43.3% accuracy on AIME 2024 with a 7B base model

facts.claim: Qwen2.5 base models improve ~60% with no template vs R1 template; template mismatch can destroy reasoning before RL starts.
facts.quote: Intriguingly, Qwen-2.5 base models get an immediate ∼ 60% improvement by not using template

conflicts: S17 (DAPO) fixes the same length problem by token-level averaging across the batch; S18 divides by a constant (e.g., max length). TRL exposes both (S59).
S15 attributes emergent reflection to RL; S18 shows it in the base model.

sources.title: Group Sequence Policy Optimization
sources.authors: Chujie Zheng, Shixuan Liu, Mingze Li, Xiong-Hui Chen, Bowen Yu, et al.
sources.authority: Originating paper for GSPO (sequence-level importance ratio and clipping), used in Qwen3 training.

facts.claim: Diagnosis: GRPO's token-level importance weights are a misapplication of importance sampling (one sample per token position), injecting high-variance noise that grows with response length and is amplified by clipping, ending in irreversible collapse.
facts.quote: we identify that the instability of GRPO stems from the fundamental misapplication and invalidation of importance sampling weights in its algorithmic design.

facts.claim: GSPO defines the importance ratio on sequence likelihood, with length normalization, and clips at the sequence level (Eq. 5).
facts.quote: GSPO defines the importance ratio based on sequence likelihood and performs sequence-level clipping, rewarding, and optimization.

facts.claim: Clipping ranges used: GSPO 3e-4 / 4e-4 (left/right); GRPO baseline tuned to 0.2 / 0.27 - the sequence-level log ratio lives on a different scale.
facts.quote: In GSPO, we set the left and right clipping ranges in Equation (5) to 3e-4 and 4e-4, respectively.

facts.claim: GRPO on MoE needs Routing Replay to converge; GSPO removes the need because sequence likelihood is insensitive to which experts a token routed to.
facts.quote: GSPO eliminates the dependency on Routing Replay and is fully capable of computing the importance ratios si (θ ) conventionally, converging normally, and optimizing stably.

facts.claim: Infrastructure angle: sequence-level likelihood tolerates training-vs-inference engine precision differences better, so rollout log-probs may not need recomputation by the training engine.
facts.quote: Given the precision discrepancies between training engines (e.g., Megatron) and inference engines (e.g., SGLang and vLLM)

conflicts: SAPO (arXiv 2511.20347, abstract verified, not entered as a source) argues GSPO suppresses an entire sequence when a few tokens are off-policy and proposes a soft token-adaptive gate.
S20 (MiniMax-M1) argues the opposite direction: keep every token's gradient and clip the IS weight (CISPO) rather than clipping updates.

sources.title: MiniMax-M1: Scaling Test-Time Compute Efficiently with Lightning Attention
sources.authors: MiniMax (Aili Chen, Aonian Li, et al.)
sources.authority: Source of CISPO and an early, concrete training-vs-inference-kernel mismatch diagnosis (FP32 LM head).

facts.claim: CISPO clips importance-sampling weights instead of token updates; full RL run of M1 took 3 weeks on 512 H800 GPUs, rental cost $534,700.
facts.quote: CISPO clips importance sampling weights rather than token updates, outperforming other competitive RL variants.

facts.claim: Why PPO/GRPO clipping hurt: rare "fork" tokens (However, Recheck, Wait, Aha) have low probability, high ratio after the first update, get clipped out and stop contributing to later off-policy updates.
facts.quote: tokens associated with reflective behaviors (e.g., However, Recheck, Wait, Aha), which often serve as “forks” in reasoning paths, were typically rare and assigned low probabilities by our base model.

facts.claim: CISPO: stop-gradient on a clipped importance weight multiplied into a REINFORCE-style term, keeping group-relative advantage and token-level loss; no PPO-style token dropping.
facts.quote: Rather than clipping the token updates as in PPO/GRPO, we instead clip the importance sampling weight in Eq. 3 to stabilize training.

facts.claim: Controlled study on Qwen2.5-32B: CISPO beats DAPO and GRPO at equal steps and matches DAPO with 50% of the steps (2x speedup).
facts.quote: achieves comparable performance to DAPO using 50% of the training steps.

facts.claim: Training/inference probability mismatch blocked reward growth in the hybrid-attention model; traced layer-by-layer to high-magnitude LM-head activations; fix: FP32 LM head realigned the two probabilities (Figure 3 right panel labels a correlation of 0.987319; the text says it rose from roughly 0.9x).
facts.quote: To address this, we increased the precision of the LM output head to FP32, thereby realigning the two theoretically identical probabilities

facts.claim: The mismatch did not appear in smaller dense softmax-attention models - it is architecture- and kernel-dependent.
facts.quote: Interestingly, this issue did not appear in smaller, dense models with softmax attention.

conflicts: S27 (FP16 paper) argues the root cause is BF16 rounding rather than any one layer and that switching to FP16 removes the mismatch; S20 fixes one layer (the LM head) in FP32.

sources.title: The Entropy Mechanism of Reinforcement Learning for Reasoning Language Models
sources.authors: Ganqu Cui, Yuchen Zhang, Jiacheng Chen, Lifan Yuan, et al.
sources.authority: Gives the empirical law and the covariance mechanism behind entropy collapse; source of Clip-Cov and KL-Cov.

facts.claim: Entropy collapses early in RL runs without intervention, yielding an over-confident policy and saturating reward.
facts.quote: where the policy entropy dropped sharply at the early training stage, leading to an overly confident policy model.

facts.claim: Empirical law R = -a*exp(H) + b between downstream performance R and entropy H: performance is "traded" from entropy, so the ceiling (H = 0, R = -a + b) is predictable.
facts.quote: the policy performance is traded from policy entropy, thus bottlenecked by its exhaustion, and the ceiling is fully predictable

facts.claim: Mechanism: entropy change is driven by the covariance between action probability and the change in logits (proportional to advantage under policy gradient). High-probability, high-advantage actions reduce entropy; rare, high-advantage actions raise it.
facts.quote: a high-probability action with high advantage would reduce policy entropy, while a rare action with high advantage would increase policy entropy.

facts.claim: Remedies: Clip-Cov (clip updates of high-covariance tokens) and KL-Cov (apply KL penalty to them).
facts.quote: we propose two simple yet effective techniques, namely Clip-Cov and KL-Cov, which clip and apply KL penalty to tokens with high covariances respectively.

conflicts: S17 (DAPO Clip-Higher) addresses the same collapse by widening the upper clip; S21 argues for token-selective control by covariance. S26 argues entropy dynamics have an exploitation phase then an exploration phase.

sources.title: The Art of Scaling Reinforcement Learning Compute for LLMs
sources.authors: Devvrit Khatri, Lovish Madaan, Rishabh Tiwari, Rachit Bansal, et al.
sources.org: Meta / UT Austin / UCL / UC Berkeley / Harvard / Periodic Labs
sources.authority: The first large-scale systematic study of RL scaling recipes (400,000+ GPU-hours); source of the ScaleRL recipe and the sigmoidal compute-performance fit.

facts.claim: Study scale and method: more than 400,000 GPU-hours; fits sigmoidal compute-vs-performance curves and ablates common design choices.
facts.quote: amounting to more than 400,000 GPU-hours, that defines a principled framework for analyzing and predicting RL scaling in LLMs.

facts.claim: Three findings: recipes differ in asymptote; loss aggregation, normalization, curriculum and off-policy algorithm mostly change compute efficiency, not the asymptote; stable recipes extrapolate from small runs.
facts.quote: Details such as loss aggregation, normalization, curriculum, and off-policy algorithm primarily modulate compute efficiency without materially shifting the asymptote

facts.claim: ScaleRL = asynchronous PipelineRL, forced length interruptions, CISPO truncated-IS loss, prompt-level loss averaging, batch-level advantage normalization, FP32 logits, zero-variance filtering, no-positive-resampling.
facts.quote: ScaleRL combines asynchronous Pipeline-RL setup (§3.1), forced length interruptions, truncated importance sampling RL loss (CISPO), prompt-level loss averaging, batch-level advantage normalization, FP32 precision at logits, zero-variance filtering, and No-Positive-Resampling

facts.claim: Validation: one run scaled to 100,000 GPU-hours on an 8B dense model (and 50k on a 17Bx16 MoE), extrapolated from fits up to 50k (16k).
facts.quote: We run ScaleRL for 100k GPU hours on an 8B dense model, and 50k GPU hours on a 17Bx16 MoE (Scout).

facts.claim: PipelineRL vs PPO-off-policy: similar asymptote, but PipelineRL reaches it faster (less idle time); optimal max off-policyness k = 8.
facts.quote: PipelineRL and PPO-off-policy achieve similar asymptotic performance A, but PipelineRL substantially improves the compute efficiency B

facts.claim: Context for scale: R1-Zero used about 100,000 H800 GPU hours of RL, 3.75% of its pre-training compute; RL compute rose more than 10x from o1 to o3 (as cited by the authors).
facts.quote: Deepseek-R1-Zero used 100,000 H800 GPU hours for RL training – 3.75% of its pre-training compute (Guo et al., 2025).

conflicts: S45 (DeepSeek-V3.2) reports a post-training budget "exceeding 10% of the pre-training cost" - a different regime from the 3.75% R1-Zero figure cited here.

sources.title: ProRL: Prolonged Reinforcement Learning Expands Reasoning Boundaries in Large Language Models
sources.authors: Mingjie Liu, Shizhe Diao, Ximing Lu, Jian Hu, Xin Dong, Yejin Choi, Jan Kautz, Yi Dong
sources.authority: The pro-"RL expands the boundary" empirical case; also the main defense of keeping a KL penalty with reference resets.

facts.claim: Claim: prolonged RL (KL control, reference-policy reset, diverse tasks) finds reasoning strategies the base model cannot reach even with extensive sampling.
facts.quote: prolonged RL (ProRL) training can uncover novel reasoning strategies that are inaccessible to base models, even under extensive sampling.

facts.claim: Gains grow with base-model weakness on the task and with training duration; RL helps most where the base model starts weak.
facts.quote: reasoning boundary improvements correlates strongly with task competence of base model and training duration

facts.claim: KL penalty justified here: explicit KL gives a more stable fix for entropy collapse than DAPO-style tricks, starting from a distilled checkpoint; "removal of KL" advice is said to apply to base models before SFT.
facts.quote: We observe that this perspective often applies to base models prior to any supervised fine-tuning.

facts.claim: Result for a 1.5B model: over 2k training steps; average pass@1 improvements over the base of 14.7% (math), 13.9% (coding), 54.8% (logic puzzles), 25.1% (STEM), 18.1% (instruction following).
facts.quote: we achieve average pass@1 improvements of 14.7% on math benchmarks, 13.9%

conflicts: S24 (Yue et al.) finds pass@k at large k shrinks after RLVR and attributes gains to sampling efficiency; S23 finds pass@k improves incl. cases where the base model fails entirely. S26 argues both are right at different training phases. Differences: S23 trains a small distilled model for >2k steps on diverse tasks; S24 evaluates shorter runs across several families.
S17 (DAPO), S48 (Olmo 3) and S47 (GLM-5) remove the KL term; S23 keeps it with periodic reference resets.

sources.title: Does Reinforcement Learning Really Incentivize Reasoning Capacity in LLMs Beyond the Base Model?
sources.authors: Yang Yue, Zhiqi Chen, Rui Lu, Andrew Zhao, Zhaokai Wang, Yang Yue, Shiji Song, Gao Huang
sources.authority: The canonical sceptical pass@k analysis of RLVR (the claim RLVR narrows rather than expands the base model's reasoning boundary).

facts.claim: RLVR-trained models beat base models at small k (pass@1) but base models win at large k; the reasoning boundary often narrows with RLVR training.
facts.quote: We observe that while RLVR-trained models outperform their base models at smaller values of k (e.g., k=1), base models achieve higher pass@k score when k is large.

facts.claim: RLVR reasoning paths already lie inside the base model's sampling distribution (coverage and perplexity analysis).
facts.quote: the reasoning paths generated by RLVR models are already included in the base models’ sampling distribution

facts.claim: Six popular RLVR algorithms perform similarly and remain far from using the base model's full potential.
facts.quote: six popular RLVR algorithms perform similarly and remain far from optimal in fully leveraging the potential of the base model.

facts.claim: Distillation, unlike RLVR, can introduce new reasoning patterns from the teacher.
facts.quote: we find that distillation can introduce new reasoning patterns from the teacher and genuinely expand the model’s reasoning capabilities.

facts.claim: Coverage of solvable problems (pass@256) decreases as pass@1 improves during RLVR training (Fig. 1 right).
facts.quote: average performance (i.e., pass@1) improves, but the coverage of solvable problems (i.e., pass@256) decreases

conflicts: S23 (ProRL) and S26 report expansion under longer or phased training; S49 (Qwen3 Table 21) reports on-policy distillation raised pass@64 while RL did not - consistent with S24 for RL, and with S24's distillation point.

sources.title: Spurious Rewards: Rethinking Training Signals in RLVR
sources.authors: Rulin Shao, Shuyue Stella Li, Rui Xin, Scott Geng, Yiping Wang, Sewoong Oh, Simon Shaolei Du, Nathan Lambert, Sewon Min, Ranjay Krishna, Yulia Tsvetkov, Hannaneh Hajishirzi, Pang Wei Koh, Luke Zettlemoyer
sources.authority: Shows RLVR gains on Qwen2.5-Math persist under random or wrong rewards, forcing a re-read of every "RLVR works on Qwen" result.

facts.claim: On Qwen2.5-Math-7B, randomly assigned rewards improved MATH-500 by 21.4 points absolute vs 29.1 points for ground-truth rewards.
facts.quote: RLVR training with GRPO improves MATH-500 performance for Qwen2.5Math-7B in absolute points by 21.4% using randomly assigned rewards, nearly matching the 29.1% gained with ground truth rewards.

facts.claim: Mechanism: GRPO's clip term creates a clipping bias that amplifies high-prior behaviours from pretraining even with uninformative rewards; the behaviour found is "code reasoning" (frequency 65% to over 90%).
facts.quote: GRPO exhibits a clipping bias arising from the clip term, which can amplify high-prior behaviors learned during pre-training even without informative rewards.

facts.claim: The effect is model-dependent: spurious rewards give minimal gain or degradation on Qwen2.5, OLMo2 and Llama3 families.
facts.quote: training with spurious rewards yields minimal improvement or even performance degradation (§3).

conflicts: S48 (Olmo 3 §2.3) cites this paper to argue open RLVR benchmarks on open-weight models with undisclosed mid-training data can be contaminated, which is why Olmo 3 releases RL-Zero from a fully open base.

sources.title: The Debate on RLVR Reasoning Capability Boundary: Shrinkage, Expansion, or Both? A Two-Stage Dynamic View
sources.authors: Xinhao Yao, Lu Yu, Xiaolin Hu, Fengwei Teng, et al.
sources.authority: Third-party reconciliation of S23 vs S24; a theoretical argument, authors' own assessment rather than consensus.

facts.claim: States the debate is unresolved and that studies split into "shrinkage" (S24) and "expansion" (S23) camps.
facts.quote: The ongoing debate on whether reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) expands or shrinks the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs) remains unresolved.

facts.claim: Proposes both are partially valid: an exploitation stage (sharpening on already-explored high-reward tokens) followed by an exploration stage (rare optimal tokens gain probability).
facts.quote: both perspectives are partially valid-each aligning with a separate phase in an inherent two-stage probability mass dynamic

sources.title: Defeating the Training-Inference Mismatch via FP16
sources.authors: Penghui Qi, Zichen Liu, Xiangxin Zhou, Tianyu Pang, Chao Du, Wee Sun Lee, Min Lin
sources.authority: Most direct treatment of the inference-engine vs training-engine numerical mismatch in RL (vLLM/SGLang rollouts vs FSDP/Megatron updates); the topic closest to Aman's inference expertise. Also summarizes the Yao et al. TIS blog (the blog itself, a Notion page, could not be fetched).

facts.claim: Claim: root cause is floating-point precision; BF16's large rounding error breaks consistency between training and inference policies; reverting to FP16 removes the mismatch with a few lines of change.
facts.quote: The widely adopted BF16, despite its large dynamic range, introduces large rounding errors that breaks the consistency between training and inference.

facts.claim: Why two engines diverge even when mathematically identical.
facts.quote: While mathematically identical, these engines produce numerically different outputs due to precision errors and hardware-specific optimizations.

facts.claim: Prior algorithmic patch: Yao et al. token-level importance sampling (TIS); it was later shown by Liu et al. to be insufficient due to biased gradient; Liu et al. proposed an unbiased sequence-level ratio (slower to converge due to variance).
facts.quote: it was later shown by Liu et al. [2025a] to be insufficient to fully stabilize training due to its biased gradient.

facts.claim: Cost of IS correction: an extra forward pass to compute the ratio, estimated at about 25% added training cost; plus a "deployment gap" because parameters are optimized for the training engine's distribution, not the inference engine's.
facts.quote: this adds approximately 25% to the training cost.

facts.claim: The deployment gap: the final weights are optimal for the training engine, not the inference engine used in serving.
facts.quote: the resulting model is not truly optimal for the inference engine used in deployment

conflicts: S20 (MiniMax-M1) fixes the mismatch with an FP32 LM head only; S47 (GLM-5) uses a deterministic top-k in the DSA indexer and IcePop masking; S45 (DeepSeek-V3.2) uses Keep Routing/Keep Sampling Mask and off-policy sequence masking; S59 (TRL) defaults to sequence-level masked importance sampling. No consensus fix.

sources.title: Scaling Laws for Reward Model Overoptimization
sources.authors: Leo Gao, John Schulman, Jacob Hilton
sources.authority: The quantitative reference for Goodhart effects in RLHF (gold-vs-proxy reward as a function of KL); cited by DeepSeek-R1 as the basis of its "no neural RMs for reasoning" choice.

facts.claim: Setup: a fixed "gold" RM stands in for humans and labels data for smaller proxy RMs, so overoptimization can be measured.
facts.quote: reward model plays the role of humans, providing labels used to train a proxy reward model.

facts.claim: Functional forms in d = sqrt(KL(pi || pi_init)): best-of-n R(d) = d(alpha_bon - beta_bon d); RL R(d) = d(alpha_RL - beta_RL log d). Coefficients scale smoothly (about logarithmically) with RM parameter count.
facts.quote: We find empirically that for best-of-n (BoN) sampling,

facts.claim: RL is slower than best-of-n in KL terms at both optimization and overoptimization, which the authors take as showing KL is an inadequate common yardstick across methods.
facts.quote: As a function of the KL divergence, reinforcement learning tends to be slower than best-of-n sampling at both optimization and overoptimization.

facts.claim: Proxy RMs of 3M to 3B parameters; gold RM is the 6B InstructGPT RM.
facts.quote: The 6B reward model from Ouyang et al. [2022] is used as the gold RM, and our proxy RMs vary from 3M to 3B parameters

sources.title: Natural Emergent Misalignment from Reward Hacking in Production RL
sources.authors: Monte MacDiarmid, Benjamin Wright, Jonathan Uesato, Joe Benton, et al.
sources.authority: Primary evidence from a frontier lab that reward hacking in RL environments can generalize to broader misalignment; names the concrete hacks.

facts.claim: Learning to reward hack in production coding RL environments generalized to alignment faking, cooperation with malicious actors, and sabotage in a Claude Code scaffold.
facts.quote: the model generalizes to alignment faking, cooperation with malicious actors, reasoning about malicious goals, and attempting sabotage when used with Claude Code

facts.claim: Chat-style RLHF safety training fixed chat evals but not agentic ones.
facts.quote: Applying RLHF safety training using standard chat-like prompts results in aligned behavior on chat-like evaluations, but misalignment persists on agentic tasks.

sources.title: Beyond Binary Rewards: Training LMs to Reason About Their Uncertainty (RLCR = Reinforcement Learning with Calibration Rewards)
sources.authors: Mehul Damani, Isha Puri, Stewart Slocum, Idan Shenfeld, Leshem Choshen, Yoon Kim, Jacob Andreas
sources.version: arXiv v2 (15 May 2026); ICLR 2026; v1 22 Jul 2025
sources.authority: The public, peer-reviewed method that trains LLMs with RL on a proper-scoring-rule reward for calibrated confidence; the nearest documented analogue to the calibration objective TypeSafe claims for RLCD. Different name, different method - do not conflate.

facts.claim: Diagnosis: binary correctness rewards do not penalize guessing, so RL degrades calibration and increases hallucination elsewhere.
facts.quote: Because such reward functions do not penalize guessing or low-confidence outputs, they often have the unintended side-effect of degrading calibration and increasing the rate at which LMs generate incorrect responses

facts.claim: Reward = binary correctness + Brier score of the verbalized confidence q: R = 1[y == y*] - (q - 1[y == y*])^2 (Eq. 1). The model emits an answer and a numeric confidence after reasoning.
facts.quote: We first prove that this reward function (or any analogous reward function that uses a bounded, proper scoring rule) yields models whose predictions are both accurate and well-calibrated.

facts.claim: Theorem 1: the expected reward is maximized when q equals the true success probability (calibration incentive), and among calibrated predictions by the answer with the highest success probability (correctness incentive).
facts.quote: Calibration incentive. For any y, the expected reward E1y≡y∗ RRLCR (y, q, y ∗ ) is maximized when q = py .

facts.claim: Log-likelihood is a proper scoring rule but unbounded, so it does not give the correctness incentive; any bounded proper scoring rule can be used.
facts.quote: Notably, log-likelihood, though a proper scoring rule, is unbounded and can incentivize models to output incorrect answers (Section 3).

facts.claim: Measured: expected calibration error 0.37 -> 0.03 on HotpotQA and 0.26 -> 0.10 on a collection of math datasets, accuracy matched to RLVR.
facts.quote: reducing expected calibration error from 0.37 → 0.03 on HotpotQA (Yang et al., 2018) and 0.26 → 0.10 on a collection of math datasets (Section 4).

facts.claim: Out of domain, RLVR worsens calibration while RLCR improves it.
facts.quote: where RLVR substantially worsens calibration generalization to new domains, RLCR improves calibration

facts.claim: Verbalized confidence can be used at test time (confidence-weighted voting) to improve accuracy and calibration.
facts.quote: verbalized confidence can be leveraged at test time to improve accuracy and calibration via confidence-weighted scaling methods.

conflicts: Name collision: RLCR (this paper) vs RLCD (S34 = Contrastive Distillation, 2023; S35 = TypeSafe Calibrated Decisions, 2026). RLCR verbalizes confidence in text; TypeSafe says its model returns typed probability distributions without generating text (S35).

sources.authority: Frontier-lab theory of why binary-graded training and evaluation reward guessing; supplies the incentive argument behind calibration-aware RL rewards.

facts.claim: Thesis: hallucinations persist because training and evaluation reward guessing over acknowledging uncertainty.
facts.quote: language models hallucinate because the training and evaluation procedures reward guessing over acknowledging uncertainty

facts.claim: Under binary (0-1) grading abstaining is strictly suboptimal; "I don't know" gets the minimum score while a best guess is optimal.
facts.quote: grading, abstaining is strictly sub-optimal. IDK-type responses are maximally penalized while an overconfident “best guess” is optimal.

facts.claim: Proposed fix is to change how existing mainstream benchmarks are scored, not to add more hallucination evals; sample prompt text with explicit confidence targets t: mistakes cost t/(1-t) points (t=0.5 -> 1, t=0.75 -> 2, t=0.9 -> 9).
facts.quote: Answer only if you are > t confident, since mistakes are penalized t/(1 − t) points, while correct answers receive 1 point, and an answer of “I don’t know” receives 0 points.

conflicts: S32 (RLCR) and S10 train the fix into the policy via a proper-scoring reward; S33 argues the fix is primarily in how benchmarks grade. Both predict binary-reward RLVR pushes toward guessing.

sources.title: RLCD: Reinforcement Learning from Contrastive Distillation for Language Model Alignment
sources.authors: Kevin Yang, Dan Klein, Asli Celikyilmaz, Nanyun Peng, Yuandong Tian
sources.version: arXiv v3 (16 Mar 2024); ICLR 2024 poster; first posted 24 Jul 2023
sources.authority: The older, unrelated "RLCD". Verified as Contrastive Distillation (some indexes print "Contrast Distillation"). Include only as a clearly labelled RLAIF improvement.

facts.claim: RLCD builds preference pairs from two contrasting prompts for the same task: a positive prompt p+ encouraging the principle and a negative prompt p- encouraging its violation; no human feedback.
facts.quote: RLCD creates preference pairs from two contrasting model outputs, one using a positive prompt designed to encourage following the given principles, and one using a negative prompt designed to encourage violating them.

facts.claim: Rationale: two different prompts make outputs more distinguishable, so automatic preference labels are cleaner than RLAIF labels on two i.i.d. samples from one prompt.
facts.quote: Using two different prompts causes model outputs to be more differentiated on average, resulting in cleaner preference labels in the absence of human annotations.

facts.quote: We then use the preference pairs to train a preference model, which is in turn used to improve a base unaligned language model via reinforcement learning.

facts.claim: No-std advantage to remove the difficulty bias.

facts.claim: Truncated importance sampling corrects the inference-engine (vLLM) vs training probability gap, following Yao et al.

facts.quote: Given the cost of autoregressive inference, our learner spends 75% of the time waiting for data, so in terms of GPU utilization, we use approximately 5x as much for inference as for training.

facts.claim: Continuous batching avoids waste: at 32K max and 14,628 mean generation length, up to 54% of compute would be wasted by static batching.
facts.quote: which means that up to 54% of our compute would have been wasted with static batching.

facts.claim: Infrastructure payoff: continuous batching + inflight updates gave two times faster training on half as many GPUs; 7B run went from about 15 days to 6 days.

sources.authority: Concrete example of procedurally generated, parametrically scaled verifiable environments - the "environment as a generator + verifier" pattern.

facts.claim: Library of over 100 task generators and verifiers across algebra, arithmetic, computation, cognition, geometry, graph theory, logic and games.
facts.quote: It provides over 100 data generators and verifiers spanning multiple domains including algebra, arithmetic, computation, cognition, geometry, graph theory, logic, and various common games.

facts.claim: Key property: effectively unlimited data with adjustable difficulty, unlike fixed datasets.
facts.quote: Its key innovation is the ability to generate virtually infinite training data with adjustable complexity, unlike most previous reasoning datasets, which are typically fixed.

facts.claim: Design principle P3: configurable parameters set problem difficulty, enabling dynamic curricula.
facts.quote: Configurable parameters systematically control problem characteristics, enabling dynamic curricula via precise difficulty adjustment.

facts.claim: Findings: sharp performance cliffs when difficulty rises; adaptive curricula beat fixed difficulty; RLVR generalizes within a domain.
facts.quote: Curriculum RLVR results in improved final models, with adaptive difficulty progression outperforming fixed-difficulty training across reasoning tasks.

sources.title: Group-in-Group Policy Optimization for LLM Agent Training (GiGPO)
sources.authors: Lang Feng, Zhenghai Xue, Tingcong Liu, Bo An
sources.authority: Representative multi-turn credit-assignment extension of GRPO that stays critic-free.

facts.claim: Problem: multi-turn agent rewards are sparse/delayed; credit assignment across steps is much harder than in single-turn math.
facts.quote: making credit assignment across individual steps significantly more challenging.

facts.claim: Method: two-level relative advantage - episode-level groups of trajectories, plus step-level groups built by finding repeated environment states ("anchor states") across trajectories; no critic, no extra rollouts.
facts.quote: At the step-level, GiGPO introduces an anchor state grouping mechanism that retroactively constructs step-level groups by identifying repeated environment states across trajectories.

facts.claim: Reported gains over GRPO: >12% on ALFWorld and >9% on WebShop (Qwen2.5-1.5B/3B/7B-Instruct).
facts.quote: achieves performance gains of > 12% on ALFWorld and > 9% on WebShop over GRPO

conflicts: Anchor-state grouping needs repeated identical states, which holds in ALFWorld/WebShop-style environments but is not guaranteed in open-ended tool use (inference from the abstract; not tested here).

sources.authority: What the most-used open trainer ships as defaults is a good proxy for current practice. Documents the dapo/dr_grpo/sapo/cispo loss variants, sequence-level importance sampling (GSPO) and vLLM mismatch correction.

facts.claim: Default loss in the docs is DAPO-style token-level normalization (loss_type default "dapo"); original GRPO per-sequence 1/|o_i| normalization is described as the initial formulation.
facts.quote: loss_type: str = 'dapo'

facts.claim: Dr. GRPO option: divide by a constant (recommended: maximum completion length) instead of sequence length.
facts.quote: This constant is recommended to be the maximum completion length.

facts.claim: SAPO option (Qwen): smooth, temperature-controlled soft gate replacing hard clipping; CISPO option also present.
facts.quote: the Qwen team proposes replacing the "hard" clipping mechanism of GRPO with a smooth, temperature-controlled soft gating mechanism.

facts.claim: Default KL coefficient is 0.0, so the reference model is not loaded (saves memory); R1's 0.001 is cited as an alternative.
facts.quote: If 0.0 (default), the reference model is not loaded, reducing memory usage and improving training speed.

facts.claim: Clip defaults: epsilon 0.2; epsilon_high None (same as epsilon); DAPO recommends 0.28; with CISPO the recommended value is 5.0.
facts.quote: Paper [DAPO] recommends 0.28.

facts.claim: Advantage scaling default is "group" (std-normalized per group); "batch" and False are options; turning off std scaling means update magnitude depends on raw reward scale.
facts.quote: Note that turning off std-based scaling also removes variance normalization, so update magnitudes depend directly on the raw reward scale and batch composition.

facts.claim: importance_sampling_level default "token"; "sequence" gives the GSPO behaviour.
facts.quote: The [GSPO paper] shows that sequence-level sampling often yields more stable training and better alignment with sequence-level rewards.

facts.claim: num_generations default 8; vLLM integration modes "colocate" (default; shares GPUs with the trainer) and "server" (separate GPUs, HTTP).
facts.quote: Number of generations per prompt to sample.

facts.claim: Mismatch handling is on by default: sequence-level masked importance sampling; TIS truncates (clip max default 3.0) while MIS zeroes outliers.
facts.quote: By default, sequence-level Masked Importance Sampling (`vllm_importance_sampling_mode="sequence_mask"`) is activated for vLLM generation to address the generation-training mismatch

conflicts: Defaults here (DAPO loss, KL 0, group-std scaling still on) mix choices that S18/S45/S48 argue against (std scaling).

sources.title: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF Book)
sources.authors: Nathan Lambert
sources.org: Allen Institute for AI; print edition Manning Publications
sources.version: arXiv v12 (11 Sep 2026); web edition "last built 14 October 2026"; Manning print July 2026 (per rlhfbook.com); v1 posted Apr 2025
sources.readDepth: table of contents, §3.1.6, §3.2.4, §7.3 (arXiv v12 text); rlhfbook.com landing page for edition facts
sources.authority: The only single-volume textbook-tier treatment spanning RLHF, RLVR, DPO, rejection sampling, MOPD and over-optimization; written by the Tulu 3 lead; updated through Sep 2026.

facts.claim: Scope as stated in the abstract.
facts.quote: The core of the book details every optimization stage in using RLHF, from starting with instruction tuning to training a reward model and finally all of rejection sampling, reinforcement learning, on-policy distillation, and direct alignment algorithms.

facts.claim: Chapter map (v12): 1 Introduction; 2 A Tiny History of RLHF; 3 Training Overview; 4 Instruction Fine-Tuning; 5 Reward Modeling; 6 Reinforcement Learning; 7 Reasoning and Inference-Time Scaling; 8 Direct-Alignment Algorithms; 9 Rejection Sampling; 10 The Nature of Preferences; 11 Preference Data; 12 Synthetic Data & Distillation; 13 Tool Use (section 13.1 Tool-Use Overview); 14 Over-Optimization; 15 Regularization; 16 Evaluation; 17 Crafting Model Character and Products.
facts.quote: 6 Reinforcement Learning

facts.claim: Author's argument for RL despite simpler alternatives (rejection sampling, DPO): RL keeps winning; costs far more infrastructure; improvements "generally help the model a lot".
facts.quote: Still, despite the simplicity of alternatives, RL-based methods continue to win out.

facts.claim: RL can be surgical: Tulu 3 trained RL on math prompts only while preserving general capability.
facts.quote: RL can be done surgically — the model does a good job of learning where the prompt distribution lies, and RL tends to not “squash” the general capabilities of the model.

facts.claim: 2026 recipe shift: MOPD became a popular merging tool; MiMo-V2-Flash first documented it; counts of experts: Nemotron 3 Ultra >10, Kimi K3 nine, DeepSeek V4 >10.
facts.quote: Various models utilizing MOPD as a final stage use a different number of experts, with Nemotron 3 Ultra at more than ten [65], Kimi K3 at nine [66], and DeepSeek V4 at more than ten [67]

facts.claim: Non-unanimity: labs are not agreed on MOPD; GLM-5 uses MOPD after a three-stage RL.
facts.quote: MOPD is a popular new tool, but labs are far from unanimous in its usage.

facts.claim: Reasoning training reduces to a large RL run or SFT on outputs of a model that underwent much RLVR (distillation).
facts.quote: traditionally for a reasoning model the core training step is either a large-scale RL run or a large-scale instruction tuning run on outputs of another model that had undergone a substantial portion of RLVR training (referred to as distillation).

conflicts: Online and print editions differ in date and layout from the arXiv v12 text; cite section numbers from the version you open.

disagreements.topic: Is DPO enough, or does online RL (PPO) win for preference tuning?

positions.claim: DPO-family methods are sufficient and cheaper at scale: Llama 3 tried PPO and found DPO needed less compute and did better on IFEval; Tulu 3 measured PPO roughly equal to DPO at about 28 h on two nodes vs about 4 h on one node and kept DPO for preference iteration.
Tuned PPO beats DPO: Xu et al. report PPO ahead on every testbed; Ivison et al. find PPO ahead by up to 2.5% (math) and 1.2% (general), but also that data quality matters more than the algorithm.
RL keeps winning despite far higher infrastructure cost, and can be applied surgically (math-only RL preserved general ability in Tulu 3).

disagreements.topic: Critic or no critic: is a value model worth it?

positions.claim: PPO's critic is unnecessary or harmful for LLMs (reward only at the last token, policy-sized memory cost): REINFORCE/RLOO, GRPO and Kimi's mean-reward baseline drop it.

A value model still carries weight in practice: Tulu 3 RLVR found initializing the value function from a general RM gave the best results and listed value-free GRPO only as future work; Xu et al. get best results from carefully configured PPO.

disagreements.topic: Does RLVR create new reasoning capability, or only sharpen what the base model can already do?

positions.claim: It sharpens: pass@k at large k is higher for base models and the boundary narrows; DeepSeekMath saw Maj@K but not Pass@K improve; Qwen3 found on-policy distillation lifted pass@64 while RL did not.
It can expand with long enough training, KL control with reference resets and diverse tasks (1.5B model, >2k steps).
Both, in phases: an exploitation stage followed by an exploration stage (theoretical reconciliation, authors' own assessment).

Much of the observed gain is prior amplification: random or wrong rewards lift Qwen2.5-Math by 21.4 MATH-500 points vs 29.1 for true rewards; templates and base-model pretraining drive R1-Zero-like results; contamination can make spurious rewards look as good as true ones.

disagreements.topic: How should the GRPO loss and advantage be normalized?

positions.claim: Original GRPO: per-sequence 1/|o_i| averaging and division by group reward std (still the TRL group-std default).
Token-level averaging across the batch (DAPO; OlmoRL; TRL loss default "dapo").
Constant normalizer and no std division, to remove length and difficulty bias (Dr. GRPO).
Keep token-level loss but drop only the std division (DeepSeek-V3.2 advantage = R - mean(R); OlmoRL).
These choices mostly move compute efficiency, not the asymptote (ScaleRL uses prompt-level loss averaging and batch-level advantage normalization).

disagreements.topic: Keep or remove the KL-to-reference term?

positions.claim: Remove it for long-CoT RL: policy must diverge; no over-optimization observed (DAPO, OlmoRL, GLM-5; TRL default beta = 0.0).
Keep it, with periodic reference resets, when starting from an SFT/distilled checkpoint: more stable than other entropy fixes; "remove KL" advice applies to raw base models.
Small, domain-dependent KL with a corrected estimator (V3.2: weak or none for math); small coefficients elsewhere (R1 0.001; DeepSeekMath 0.04; Tulu 3 0.05-0.07).

disagreements.topic: Importance ratio and clipping: token-level, sequence-level, IS-weight clipping, or soft gating?

positions.claim: Token-level PPO-style clip, widened on the upside (Clip-Higher 0.2/0.28).
Sequence-level ratio and clipping (GSPO), which removes the need for MoE routing replay and tolerates train/inference numeric differences.
Clip the importance weight, not the update, so low-probability "fork" tokens keep contributing gradients (CISPO; adopted inside ScaleRL).
Mask tokens by log-ratio outside [alpha, beta] regardless of advantage sign (Kimi K2.5); per-token regularization tolerates staleness (K3).
Asymmetric clipping (Clip-Higher) plus dynamic sampling / active sampling.
Covariance-selective control: Clip-Cov / KL-Cov on tokens with high probability-advantage covariance.
KL penalty with reference resets and higher temperature.
Sampling temperature decay from exploration to exploitation.

disagreements.topic: Fixing the training-inference mismatch (vLLM/SGLang rollout vs trainer): algorithm, numerics, or determinism?

positions.claim: Correct statistically with importance sampling (truncated or masked; token or sequence level).
Fix numerics: FP32 LM head (MiniMax-M1; ScaleRL) or FP16 instead of BF16.
Remove the source: reuse sampling-time MoE routing and top-p/top-k masks (DeepSeek-V3.2), deterministic indexer top-k plus IcePop masking (GLM-5).
Mask highly off-policy negative-advantage sequences using the inference engine's own probabilities.

disagreements.topic: Learned reward models, verifiers, or generative/rubric judges?

positions.claim: Avoid neural reward models on reasoning tasks because they are hacked during large-scale RL; use rule-based verifiers.
Use generative/rubric judges for non-verifiable tasks: Kimi self-critic rubric reward and GRMs, per-prompt rubrics in V3.2, rubric-guided GRM in V4, Rubrics-as-Rewards.
Train the judge inside the same RL loop (actor doubles as GRM in V4; critic refined on verifiable rollouts in K2; agentic judge protocol in K3).
Process supervision beats outcome supervision for reward models on MATH.
At RL scale PRMs are impractical: hard step definition, hard step verification, hackable.
Stepwise reward models remain useful for filtering SFT traces.
Step-level credit without a learned PRM, via anchor-state grouping in multi-turn tasks.

disagreements.topic: How to combine many skills: single mixed RL, sequential stages, or specialists + on-policy distillation?

positions.claim: Merge reasoning, agent and alignment RL into one mixed stage to avoid forgetting (DeepSeek-V3.2), or one unified RLVR run before distillation (Nemotron 3 Ultra).
Train domain experts with RL, then replace mixed RL entirely with multi-teacher on-policy distillation (DeepSeek-V4, Kimi K3 with nine experts, MOPD paper).
Multi-stage RL with cross-stage distillation (GLM-5); four-stage pipeline plus strong-to-weak distillation for small models (Qwen3).
Labs are not unanimous; MOPD has open issues on long-horizon agentic rollouts.

disagreements.topic: RL or distillation for strong small reasoning models?

positions.claim: Distill: R1 found 10K+ steps of RL on Qwen2.5-32B only matched QwQ-32B-Preview while distilling R1 did better; Qwen3 and Thinking Machines report on-policy distillation about 1/10 the GPU hours of RL (17,920 vs 1,800 GPU-hours, Qwen3-8B).

RL is still needed to push beyond the teacher / frontier ("advancing beyond the boundaries of human intelligence may still require more powerful base models and larger-scale reinforcement learning") and ProRL reports gains beyond a distilled start.
Length penalty, warmed up after standard RL (Kimi k1.5); soft overlong punishment (DAPO).
Per-sample or per-problem token budgets as a reward override (K2, K3), alternating budget-limited and unconstrained phases (Toggle: -25 to -30% tokens).
Train separate experts per reasoning-effort mode with distinct length penalties and contexts (V4, K3 low/high/max).
Fix the length bias in the loss itself rather than adding a penalty (Dr. GRPO).

disagreements.topic: Calibration: train it into the policy, or fix how benchmarks grade?

positions.claim: Add a bounded proper-scoring-rule term (Brier) to the RL reward; calibration error 0.37 -> 0.03 on HotpotQA with matched accuracy.
Primary fix is socio-technical: stop 0-1 grading that penalizes abstention; add explicit confidence targets to benchmark instructions.

disagreements.topic: TypeSafe "RLCD": new post-training regime, or a rebranding of known calibration-aware RL?

positions.claim: Company position: RLHF causes sycophancy, mode dropping and overconfidence; RLCD yields typed outputs with calibrated probabilities (fast, cheap, "can't hallucinate" at the type level); RLHF is "please humans", RLVR is "optimize benchmarks", RLCD is "make it reliable for programmatic use".

Public literature already shows binary-reward RLVR degrades calibration and that proper-scoring-rule rewards repair it in ordinary text-generating models; an independent reconstruction (score each rationale's answer distribution with a proper score) exists but is not TypeSafe's method.

Outside assessment is mixed and unverified: a developer says it "delegates the hallucination problem a little bit to the user"; one tester found Gemini slightly more accurate; company accuracy parity is scored against the average of two frontier LLMs' outputs rather than ground truth; no published benchmarks.

RLCD FINDING. "Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions (RLCD)" by TypeSafe AI IS real as a company-asserted method, but there is no paper, repo, reward function, or algorithm. Primary statements: launch post by Diogo Almeida dated 15 Sep 2026 (S36), docs.typesafe.ai "AI primer" (S35), founder interview (S37). The only third-party coverage is TechCrunch 18 Sep 2026 (S38), which writes "from" not "for" calibrated decisions. Public technical content under the name RLCD is third-party and independent: OpenJev-RLCD (arXiv 2609.38850, S39) is a re-derivation (score each sampled rationale's answer distribution with a strictly proper scoring rule; "calibrate, then reinforce"; Qwen3-1.7B) that says explicitly TypeSafe discloses no algorithm; arXiv 2609.28940 (S40) and arXiv 2609.29429 ("Just Ask Jev", abstract verified, not entered) use the term. The founder says RLCD is unpublished, declines to explain it, and says "it's not about the PPO". Therefore the planner may schedule an RLCD module only as: (1) what is claimed and by whom, with the vendor/independent distinction; (2) the public, verifiable machinery it most plausibly resembles (RLCR S32, Behaviorally Calibrated RL S10, Kalai et al. S33, proper scoring rules); (3) the OpenJev reconstruction labelled as a reconstruction. It must NOT present a TypeSafe reward function or algorithm. Question for Aman at the checkpoint: does he accept this framing, or did he mean RLCR or another method? Searches run (WebSearch): "Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions RLCD"; "TypeSafeAI RLCD reinforcement learning calibrated decisions LLM"; "TypeSafeAI github"; "RLCD arxiv 2026 calibrated decisions ..."; "TechCrunch TypeSafe Jev ..."; plus direct fetches of typesafe.ai pages, docs.typesafe.ai (llms.txt index lists no research/training page), and the TypeSafe blog index (five posts; none discloses RLCD detail). GitHub: github.com/typesafe-ai (official: SDKs, adapter, skills) and github.com/TypeSafeAI (an unofficial community org that says it does not speak for the company); neither has RLCD training code. Date oddity: every TypeSafe blog page carries metadata date 19 Oct 2026 (export timestamp) while headers show 9-15 Sep / 9-14 Oct. Company funding statement in S36 sibling post: $870M series A at $7.5B valuation (a footnote); a launch post body reads "we raised $$$" as a placeholder.

NAME COLLISIONS. RLCD (Yang et al., ICLR 2024) = Reinforcement Learning from Contrastive Distillation, arXiv 2307.12950 (S34, verified: authors Kevin Yang, Dan Klein, Asli Celikyilmaz, Nanyun Peng, Yuandong Tian; some indexes print "Contrast"). RLCD (TypeSafe, 2026) = Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions (S35, S36). RLCR (Damani et al., ICLR 2026) = Reinforcement Learning with Calibration Rewards, arXiv 2507.16806 (S32). RLHV = Barbosa's proposal in S40. Coordinator's recollection of the older RLCD (Yang et al., 2023/ICLR 2024) is CONFIRMED.

COORDINATOR NOTE 4 CASE STUDIES. Selected because each has a primary technical report read in part: (1) DeepSeek-R1 (S15) - mandatory; R1-Zero, GRPO, rule-based RLVR, cost, failed PRM/MCTS.
